lessons.title: Macros with Arguments
intro: #define can take arguments: #define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x)). Before the compiler starts, the preprocessor replaces SQUARE(n) with ((n) * (n)). It pastes text; it doesn't calculate anything.
That's why the brackets matter. With #define BAD(x) x * x, BAD(1 + 2) becomes 1 + 2 * 1 + 2, which is 5. The rule: brackets around every parameter, and around the whole thing.
A macro costs nothing at run time, because there is no function call. But an argument can be used twice: SQUARE(i++) adds 1 to i twice. Modern C often uses small functions instead.

exercises.prompt: What does the preprocessor do with SQUARE(n)?
options: Pastes ((n) * (n)) into the code before compiling
Calls a function at run time
Checks that n is a number
exercises.explanation: Macros are text replacement. The compiler only sees the result.

exercises.prompt: Finish the macro so it's safe with any argument.
exercises.explanation: Every parameter gets its own brackets.

exercises.prompt: This program prints 6, but it should print 12. Which line is wrong?
#define MAX(a, b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b)) What's the problem with MAX(i++, j)?
exercises.explanation: If i++ is bigger, it's pasted in twice: once in the comparison, once as the result.

code: #define SWAP(a, b) { int t = a; a = b; b = t; }
exercises.explanation: A macro can be a whole block of statements. It swaps x and y.

lessons.title: #ifdef and #if 0
intro: The preprocessor can switch lines on and off before compiling. Code between #ifdef DEBUG and #endif is only kept if DEBUG is defined.
That's how programmers keep their debug printfs: delete one #define, and they're all gone from the program. #ifndef means "if not defined", and #else gives the other choice.
#if 0 … #endif switches a whole block off. C programmers use it to comment out code, because it even works around code that has /* comments */ inside.

exercises.explanation: FRENCH is never defined, so only the #else part is compiled.

options: Removes the lines between it before compiling
Runs the lines 0 times in a loop
exercises.explanation: 0 means false, so the block is never compiled.
#ifdef DEBUG keeps the line only when DEBUG is defined.

exercises.prompt: How do you switch all the DEBUG printfs off at once?
exercises.explanation: Without the #define, every #ifdef DEBUG block disappears.

exercises.prompt: Put the lines in order so the message only appears in a debug build.
exercises.explanation: Open the block with #ifdef, close it with #endif.

options: Keep the lines only if X is NOT defined
Keep the lines if X is 0
exercises.explanation: The n stands for "not". It's used for include guards, in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Header Files
intro: Real programs are split into several .c files. A header file (.h) lists what the others may use: function prototypes, typedefs and #defines. Each .c file #includes it. stdio.h is exactly that: the prototypes for printf and friends.

So a header can be included twice without errors, it starts with an include guard: #ifndef STACK_H, #define STACK_H, … and #endif at the end. The second time, STACK_H is already defined and everything is skipped.

static in front of a global variable or function makes it private to its file. You compile all the files together with cc main.c stack.c, and the linker joins them. Here, all three files are shown in one, separated by comments.

code: /* ---- stack.h: what other files may use ---- */

exercises.prompt: What belongs in a header file?
options: Prototypes, typedefs and #defines that other files need
exercises.explanation: The header says what exists; the .c file says how it works.

exercises.prompt: What is an include guard for?
options: It stops a header from being included twice
exercises.explanation: Headers include other headers, so the same one can easily come in twice.
The first time, SCORE_H isn't defined yet: the header defines it and is read. The second time, it's skipped.

exercises.prompt: static int top; at the top of stack.c means:
options: Only code in stack.c can use top
exercises.explanation: main.c can't touch the stack's insides: it has to use push and pop.

exercises.prompt: How do you compile a program made of main.c and stack.c?
options: cc main.c, which finds stack.c by itself
exercises.explanation: Each .c file is compiled, then the linker joins them into one program.

options: <…> is for system headers, "…" for your own files
exercises.explanation: With quotes, the compiler looks in your own folder first.
